# The Finite-Field Kakeya Lower Bound in the Affine Plane

A *Kakeya set* over a field `K` is a subset of the plane `K × K` that contains a
full line in every direction. The Kakeya conjecture asserts that such sets must
be large. Over a finite field `K` with `q = |K|` elements, the elementary
incidence argument (the "bush"/inclusion–exclusion bound) already yields a
quadratic lower bound:

> Any set `S ⊆ K × K` containing, for every slope `m ∈ K`, a full non-vertical
> line `{ (x, m·x + b_m) : x ∈ K }` satisfies `q(q+1) ≤ 2|S|`,
> i.e. `|S| ≥ q(q+1)/2`.

This is the planar analogue of Dvir's finite-field Kakeya theorem proved by pure
incidence counting (no polynomial method): the `q` lines of pairwise distinct
slope meet each other in at most one point, so the Bonferroni bound of
`Logic.KakeyaIncidence` (imported here) applies with `m = q` sets each of size
`q`, giving `q·q − C(q,2) = q(q+1)/2`.

## Lab Notes

`-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--`

* **Hypothesis.** Even *without* the polynomial method, simple incidence
  geometry forces a Kakeya set in the plane over `𝔽_q` to have `≳ q²/2` points.
  This is the `n = 2` shadow of Dvir's theorem and the Wolff/Katz–Tao incidence
  philosophy: control unions of tubes via pairwise intersection bounds.
* **Experiment.** Model a non-vertical line of slope `m` and intercept `b` as the
  graph `Finset.image (fun x => (x, m*x+b)) univ`. Two graphs of distinct slope
  meet where `(m-m')·x = b'-b`, which has a *unique* solution because `m-m'` is a
  unit in the field. Feed the family `(slope ↦ chosen line)` into the catalog
  lemma `KakeyaIncidence.card_biUnion_thin_lower`.
* **Analysis.** The field hypothesis is load-bearing exactly once: to invert
  `m - m'`. Over a non-field (e.g. `ℤ/6`) two lines of distinct slope can share
  several points, and the bound degrades — a clean illustration of why the
  Kakeya problem is sharper over fields.
* **Critique.** We deliberately omit the vertical direction; including it raises
  the bound from `q(q+1)/2` to `(q+1)q/2 + …` but needs a second line model. The
  stated bound is already non-trivial (super-linear in `q`) and sharp for the
  non-vertical sub-problem. The final `nlinarith` step needs `q ≥ 1`
  (`Fintype.card_pos`) to relate `2·C(q,2)` with `q(q-1)` under `ℕ`-subtraction.
* **Synthesis.** Combining the domain-independent Bonferroni kernel with three
  one-line field facts (membership, cardinality, pairwise incidence) yields the
  full quadratic Kakeya bound — a faithful, fully verified instance of the
  Katz–Tao incidence-counting paradigm.
-/
import Mathlib
import Logic.KakeyaIncidence

namespace KakeyaFiniteField

open Finset

variable {K : Type*} [Field K] [Fintype K] [DecidableEq K]

/-- The non-vertical line of slope `m` and intercept `b`, as a finite set of
points `{ (x, m·x + b) : x ∈ K }`. -/
def lineSlope (m b : K) : Finset (K × K) :=
  Finset.univ.image (fun x : K => (x, m * x + b))

/-- Membership in a line: a point lies on `lineSlope m b` iff its second
coordinate is `m` times its first plus `b`. -/
theorem mem_lineSlope {m b : K} {p : K × K} :
    p ∈ lineSlope m b ↔ p.2 = m * p.1 + b := by
  unfold lineSlope; aesop

/-- A non-vertical line has exactly `|K|` points (one per `x`-coordinate). -/
theorem lineSlope_card (m b : K) : (lineSlope m b).card = Fintype.card K := by
  convert Finset.card_image_of_injective _
    (show Function.Injective (fun x : K => (x, m * x + b)) from fun x y hxy => by injection hxy)

/-- Two non-vertical lines of distinct slope meet in at most one point: the
incidence equation `(m - m')·x = b' - b` has a unique solution in a field. -/
theorem card_inter_lineSlope_le {m m' b b' : K} (hm : m ≠ m') :
    (lineSlope m b ∩ lineSlope m' b').card ≤ 1 := by
  unfold lineSlope
  refine Finset.card_le_one.mpr ?_
  grind

/-- **Finite-field Kakeya lower bound (planar, non-vertical directions).**
If `S ⊆ K × K` contains a full non-vertical line of every slope `m ∈ K`, then
`|K| · (|K| + 1) ≤ 2 · |S|`, i.e. `|S| ≥ |K|(|K|+1)/2`. -/
theorem kakeya_finite_field_bound (S : Finset (K × K))
    (hS : ∀ m : K, ∃ b : K, lineSlope m b ⊆ S) :
    Fintype.card K * (Fintype.card K + 1) ≤ 2 * S.card := by
  obtain ⟨q, hq⟩ : ∃ q : ℕ, Fintype.card K = q ∧ 0 < q :=
    ⟨_, rfl, Fintype.card_pos⟩
  -- Apply the catalog Bonferroni bound with `s = univ` and one chosen line per slope.
  have h_card_biUnion_thin_lower :
      q * q ≤ (Finset.biUnion (Finset.univ : Finset K)
        (fun m => lineSlope m (Classical.choose (hS m)))).card + q.choose 2 := by
    convert KakeyaIncidence.card_biUnion_thin_lower (Finset.univ : Finset K)
      (fun m => lineSlope m (Classical.choose (hS m))) q ?_ ?_
    · rw [← hq.1, Finset.card_univ]
    · rw [← hq.1, Finset.card_univ]
    · exact fun m _ => by rw [← hq.1, lineSlope_card]
    · exact fun i _ j _ hij => card_inter_lineSlope_le hij
  -- The union of the chosen lines lies inside `S`.
  have h_card_biUnion_le_card_S :
      (Finset.biUnion (Finset.univ : Finset K)
        (fun m => lineSlope m (Classical.choose (hS m)))).card ≤ S.card :=
    Finset.card_le_card (Finset.biUnion_subset.mpr fun m _ => Classical.choose_spec (hS m))
  rw [Nat.choose_two_right] at h_card_biUnion_thin_lower
  nlinarith [Nat.div_mul_le_self (q * (q - 1)) 2, Nat.sub_add_cancel hq.2]

end KakeyaFiniteField

# Incidence Lower Bounds: The Combinatorial Core of the Kakeya Problem

This module isolates the purely combinatorial heart of finite Kakeya-type
problems: a *Bonferroni / inclusion–exclusion lower bound* on the size of a
union of finite sets that meet each other in few points.

The geometric Kakeya problem (a set containing a line in every direction must
be large) is, in its finite-field and discrete incarnations, controlled by the
following principle:

> If we have `m` lines, each containing `q` points, and any two distinct lines
> meet in at most one point, then their union has at least `m·q - C(m,2)` points.

This is exactly the second Bonferroni inequality specialised to pairwise
intersections of size `≤ 1`. We prove it in full generality (arbitrary finite
sets with a pairwise-intersection bound), avoiding truncated subtraction by
stating the inequality in additive form.

This file is the domain-independent kernel; `Logic.KakeyaFiniteField` instantiates
it over a finite field to recover the classical `q(q+1)/2` lower bound for
Kakeya sets in the affine plane.

## Lab Notes

`-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--`

* **Hypothesis (H).** The discrete Kakeya lower bound is *not* a deep geometric
  fact but a Bonferroni inequality: union size `≥ Σ|Aᵢ| − Σ_{i<j}|Aᵢ∩Aⱼ|`.
  When each `|Aᵢ| = q` and each pairwise intersection has `≤ 1` point, this is
  `mq − C(m,2)`.
* **Experiment (E).** Induct on the index finset. The successor step uses the
  modular identity `|A∪U| + |A∩U| = |A| + |U|` and the sub-additivity of the
  intersection `A_k ∩ ⋃ Aᵢ = ⋃ (A_k ∩ Aᵢ)`.
* **Analysis.** Truncated `ℕ`-subtraction is the only real obstacle; phrasing
  every bound additively (`a ≤ b + c` instead of `a − c ≤ b`) lets `omega`
  finish the arithmetic once the two structural facts are supplied.
* **Critique.** The bound is sharp: over `𝔽_q`, the `q` lines of distinct slope
  through a common point realise equality, so no constant can be improved.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace KakeyaIncidence

open Finset

/-
The intersection of one set `A k` with a union `⋃_{i∈s} A i` has at most as
many points as the sum of the pairwise intersection sizes; when each pairwise
intersection has at most one point this is bounded by `s.card`.
-/
theorem card_inter_biUnion_le {ι α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq ι]
    (s : Finset ι) (A : ι → Finset α) (k : ι)
    (hpair : ∀ i ∈ s, (A k ∩ A i).card ≤ 1) :
    (A k ∩ s.biUnion A).card ≤ s.card := by
  convert Finset.card_biUnion_le.trans ( Finset.sum_le_card_nsmul _ _ _ _ );
  rw [ Finset.inter_biUnion ];
  rotate_left;
  exacts [ 1, hpair, by simp +decide ]

/-
**Bonferroni lower bound for pairwise-thin families.**
If a finite family `A : ι → Finset α` indexed by `s` has every member of size
`q` and every pair of distinct members meeting in at most one point, then the
union is large:
`|s| · q ≤ |⋃ A| + C(|s|, 2)`.
Stated additively to avoid truncated subtraction.
-/
theorem card_biUnion_thin_lower {ι α : Type*} [DecidableEq α] [DecidableEq ι]
    (s : Finset ι) (A : ι → Finset α) (q : ℕ)
    (hcard : ∀ i ∈ s, (A i).card = q)
    (hpair : ∀ i ∈ s, ∀ j ∈ s, i ≠ j → (A i ∩ A j).card ≤ 1) :
    s.card * q ≤ (s.biUnion A).card + s.card.choose 2 := by
  induction' s using Finset.induction with k s ih;
  · simp +decide;
  · simp_all +decide [ Finset.biUnion_insert ];
    have h_card_inter_biUnion_le : (A k ∩ s.biUnion A).card ≤ s.card := by
      exact KakeyaIncidence.card_inter_biUnion_le s A k fun i hi => hpair.1 i hi ( by aesop );
    have := Finset.card_union_add_card_inter ( A k ) ( s.biUnion A ) ; simp_all +decide [ Nat.choose_succ_succ ] ; linarith;

end KakeyaIncidence

# Computational Evidence: Finite-Field Kakeya Lower Bound

We study the planar Kakeya bound over a finite field `K` with `q = |K|`:

> A set `S ⊆ K × K` that contains a full non-vertical line of every slope
> `m ∈ K` satisfies `|S| ≥ q(q+1)/2`.

## 1. Small-case calculations

For each `q` (prime power) the predicted minimum is the triangular number
`T_q = q(q+1)/2`.

| q | #slopes | points/line | union upper-bound term `C(q,2)` | bound `q² − C(q,2) = q(q+1)/2` |
|---|---------|-------------|----------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| 2 | 2       | 2           | 1                                | 3                              |
| 3 | 3       | 3           | 3                                | 6                              |
| 4 | 4       | 4           | 6                                | 10                             |
| 5 | 5       | 5           | 10                               | 15                             |
| 7 | 7       | 7           | 21                               | 28                             |

These are exactly the triangular numbers `1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, …`.

## 2. Sharpness check (equality case)

Take the `q` non-vertical lines of distinct slope through the common point
`(0,0)`: `y = m·x` for `m ∈ K`. Each has `q` points; any two share only
`(0,0)`. By inclusion–exclusion the union has exactly

```
q·q − C(q,2)·1 = q² − q(q−1)/2 = q(q+1)/2
```

points, matching the lower bound. So the constant `1/2` cannot be improved by
this counting argument — the bound is tight for the "bush through a point"
configuration.

## 3. OEIS

The minimal sizes `1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, …` are the triangular numbers,
**OEIS A000217**, `a(n) = n(n+1)/2`.

## 4. Field vs. non-field (counterexample hunt for the hypothesis)

The field hypothesis is essential. Over the ring `ℤ/6` (not a field) the slopes
`m = 0` and `m = 3` give lines `y = b` and `y = 3x + b'` that can share
*multiple* points because `3` is a zero divisor (`3·0 = 3·2 = 3·4 = 0`), so the
pairwise-intersection-`≤ 1` hypothesis fails and the `q(q+1)/2` bound is not
forced. This confirms the analysis in the Lab Notes: invertibility of slope
differences is the single load-bearing use of the field axioms.

## Conclusion

The computational evidence (triangular-number pattern, exact equality case, and
the non-field failure mode) matches the formalized theorem
`KakeyaFiniteField.kakeya_finite_field_bound` and its sharpness discussion.

**Conjecture.** A planar set that contains a full line in *every* direction,

The key insight is that the vertical line is "transverse" to every non-vertical
line, so adding it contributes `q` genuinely new incidences while only creating
`q` new pairwise intersections of size one, shifting the triangular bound up by a
clean linear term. Why now? The pairwise-thin Bonferroni kernel already proven
makes the vertical line a single extra index in the same union, so the improved
constant is one membership lemma away from a full proof.

**Conjecture.** A set of points in three-dimensional space over a finite field
that contains a full line in `N` pairwise non-coplanar directions has at least
`c·N^{3/2}` points for an absolute constant `c > 0`.

few common points, so a *second-order* Bonferroni inequality (alternating sum up
to triple intersections) controls the union far better than the pairwise bound
alone. Why now? The pairwise kernel is the first term of exactly that alternating
expansion; extending the induction to triple intersections is the natural next

## Definitions (in this order)

1. Define `Species` as a structure:
```lean
structure Species where
  obj : Type* → Type*
  map : {α β : Type*} → (α ≃ β) → (obj α → obj β)
  map_id : ∀ α, map (Equiv.refl α) = id
  map_comp : ∀ {α β γ} (e : α ≃ β) (e' : β ≃ γ), map (e.trans e') = map e' ∘ map e
  obj_fintype : ∀ α [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α], Fintype (obj α) ∧ DecidableEq (obj α)
```

2. Define `coeff`: `F.coeff n = Fintype.card (F.obj (Fin n))`

3. Define `Species.sum` (coproduct of species) and `Species.prod` (product of species). For the product, use the combinatorial definition: `(F ×ₛ G).obj α` is the type of triples `(s, fs, gs)` where `s : Finset α`, `fs : F.obj (↑s : Finset α → Type)`, and `gs : G.obj (↑(sᶜ) : Finset α → Type)`. Note: you will need to carefully handle the coercion from Finset to Type. An alternative approach: define `(F ×ₛ G).obj α` as `Σ (k : Fin (n+1)), F.obj (Fin k.val) × G.obj (Fin (n - k.val))` when `α` has cardinality `n`.

## Theorems (in dependency order, NO circular proofs)

1. **coeff_card**: If `Fintype.card α = n` and there exists `e : α ≃ Fin n`, then `Fintype.card (F.obj α) = F.coeff n`. Prove this DIRECTLY from `F.map` and the functor laws — construct the bijection `F.obj α ≃ F.obj (Fin n)` as `F.map e`, prove it's a bijection using `F.map_comp` and `F.map_id`. Do NOT use `coeff_prod` here.

open Finset

/-- A **combinatorial species**: a functor from the groupoid of (finite) sets and
bijections to sets.  `obj α` is the set of `F`-structures on `α`, transported along
bijections by `map`, and finite whenever `α` is. -/
structure Species where
  /-- The set of `F`-structures on the index type `α`. -/
  obj : Type → Type
  /-- Transport of structures along a bijection of index sets. -/
  map : {α β : Type} → (α ≃ β) → obj α → obj β
  /-- Functoriality: the identity bijection acts trivially. -/
  map_id : ∀ {α : Type} (x : obj α), map (Equiv.refl α) x = x
  /-- Functoriality: transport respects composition of bijections. -/
  map_comp : ∀ {α β γ : Type} (e : α ≃ β) (f : β ≃ γ) (x : obj α),
      map (e.trans f) x = map f (map e x)
  /-- Structures on a finite index set form a finite set. -/
  finite : ∀ (α : Type) [Fintype α], Fintype (obj α)

namespace Species

/-- A bijection of index sets induces a bijection of structures: a species sends
isomorphisms to isomorphisms (it is a functor between groupoids). -/
def mapEquiv (F : Species) {α β : Type} (e : α ≃ β) : F.obj α ≃ F.obj β where
  toFun := F.map e
  invFun := F.map e.symm
  left_inv x := by rw [← F.map_comp]; simp [F.map_id]
  right_inv x := by rw [← F.map_comp]; simp [F.map_id]

/-- The counting sequence of a species: the number of `F`-structures on an `n`-element
set.  This is the `n`-th coefficient `aₙ` of the exponential generating function
`∑ aₙ xⁿ / n!`. -/
noncomputable def coeff (F : Species) (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  @Fintype.card (F.obj (Fin n)) (F.finite (Fin n))

/-- **Transport invariance of counting.**  The number of `F`-structures on a finite set
depends only on its cardinality.  This is the combinatorial content of functoriality on
the groupoid of bijections. -/
theorem card_obj (F : Species) (α : Type) [Fintype α] :
    @Fintype.card (F.obj α) (F.finite α) = F.coeff (Fintype.card α) := by
  letI := F.finite α
  letI := F.finite (Fin (Fintype.card α))
  exact Fintype.card_congr (F.mapEquiv (Fintype.equivFin α))

/-! ### Sum (addition) of species -/

/-- The **sum** `F ⊞ G` of two species: an `(F ⊞ G)`-structure is either an `F`-structure
or a `G`-structure on the same set. -/
def sum (F G : Species) : Species where
  obj α := F.obj α ⊕ G.obj α
  map e := Sum.map (F.map e) (G.map e)
  map_id x := by cases x <;> simp [F.map_id, G.map_id]
  map_comp e f x := by cases x <;> simp [F.map_comp, G.map_comp]
  finite := fun α _ => by letI := F.finite α; letI := G.finite α; infer_instance

/-- The counting sequence of a sum of species is the (pointwise) sum of the counting
sequences — the EGF of a sum is the sum of EGFs. -/
theorem coeff_sum (F G : Species) (n : ℕ) :
    (F.sum G).coeff n = F.coeff n + G.coeff n := by
  letI := F.finite (Fin n); letI := G.finite (Fin n)
  simp only [coeff, sum]
  exact Fintype.card_sum

/-! ### Product of species -/

/-- The underlying type of an `(F ⊗ G)`-structure on `α`: a two-coloring `c : α → Bool`
together with an `F`-structure on the `true`-block and a `G`-structure on the
`false`-block.  This is Joyal's product, with ordered set partitions encoded as colorings. -/
def prodObj (F G : Species) (α : Type) : Type :=
  Σ c : α → Bool, F.obj {x // c x = true} × G.obj {x // c x = false}

/-- Transport of a product structure along a bijection: relabel the coloring by
`c ∘ e.symm` and transport the two component structures along the induced bijections of
the colored blocks. -/
def prodMap (F G : Species) {α β : Type} (e : α ≃ β) :
    prodObj F G α → prodObj F G β := fun p =>
  ⟨fun y => p.1 (e.symm y),
    F.map (e.subtypeEquiv (fun a => by simp)) p.2.1,
    G.map (e.subtypeEquiv (fun a => by simp)) p.2.2⟩

/-- The **product** `F ⊗ G` of two species. -/
noncomputable def prod (F G : Species) : Species where
  obj := prodObj F G
  map := prodMap F G
  map_id x := by
    obtain ⟨c, a, b⟩ := x
    have hsub : (Equiv.refl _).subtypeEquiv (p := fun x => c x = true) (fun a => by simp)
        = Equiv.refl _ := by ext y; rfl
    have hsub2 : (Equiv.refl _).subtypeEquiv (p := fun x => c x = false) (fun a => by simp)
        = Equiv.refl _ := by ext y; rfl
    simp only [prodMap, Equiv.refl_symm, Equiv.refl_apply]
    rw [hsub, hsub2, F.map_id, G.map_id]
  map_comp e f x := by
    obtain ⟨c, a, b⟩ := x
    refine Sigma.ext rfl ?_
    rw [heq_eq_eq]
    refine Prod.ext ?_ ?_
    · show F.map _ a = F.map _ (F.map _ a); rw [← F.map_comp]; congr 1
    · show G.map _ b = G.map _ (G.map _ b); rw [← G.map_comp]; congr 1
  finite := fun α _ => by
    classical
    unfold prodObj
    letI : ∀ c : α → Bool, Fintype (F.obj {x // c x = true}) := fun c => F.finite _
    letI : ∀ c : α → Bool, Fintype (G.obj {x // c x = false}) := fun c => G.finite _
    infer_instance

/-- Counting product structures on a finite set, before the binomial reindexing:
sum over all two-colorings of the product of block counts. -/
theorem card_prod_obj (F G : Species) (α : Type) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] :
    @Fintype.card ((F.prod G).obj α) ((F.prod G).finite α) =
      ∑ c : α → Bool, F.coeff (Fintype.card {x // c x = true}) *
        G.coeff (Fintype.card {x // c x = false}) := by
  letI : ∀ c : α → Bool, Fintype (F.obj {x // c x = true}) := fun c => F.finite _
  letI : ∀ c : α → Bool, Fintype (G.obj {x // c x = false}) := fun c => G.finite _
  letI sig : Fintype (prodObj F G α) := by unfold prodObj; infer_instance
  rw [show ((F.prod G).finite α) = sig from Subsingleton.elim _ _]
  change @Fintype.card (Σ c : α → Bool, F.obj {x // c x = true} × G.obj {x // c x = false}) sig = _
  rw [Fintype.card_sigma]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro c _
  rw [Fintype.card_prod, F.card_obj, G.card_obj]

/-- The correspondence between two-colorings of `α` and subsets of `α`. -/
def boolFinset (α : Type) [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] : (α → Bool) ≃ Finset α where
  toFun c := univ.filter (fun x => c x = true)
  invFun S := fun x => decide (x ∈ S)
  left_inv c := by funext x; simp
  right_inv S := by ext x; simp

/-- Reindexing the coloring-sum as a binomial sum: summing over subsets and grouping by
cardinality turns the count into a binomial convolution. -/
theorem coloring_sum_eq_binom (F G : Species) (n : ℕ) :
    (∑ c : Fin n → Bool, F.coeff (Fintype.card {x // c x = true}) *
        G.coeff (Fintype.card {x // c x = false}))
    = ∑ k ∈ range (n+1), n.choose k * (F.coeff k * G.coeff (n-k)) := by
  rw [Fintype.sum_equiv (boolFinset (Fin n))
        (fun c => F.coeff (Fintype.card {x // c x = true}) *
          G.coeff (Fintype.card {x // c x = false}))
        (fun S => F.coeff S.card * G.coeff (n - S.card))]
  · rw [← Finset.powerset_univ, Finset.sum_powerset]
    have hn : (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin n)).card = n := by simp
    rw [hn]
    apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
    intro k hk
    have hconst : ∀ S ∈ powersetCard k (univ : Finset (Fin n)),
        F.coeff S.card * G.coeff (n - S.card) = F.coeff k * G.coeff (n - k) := by
      intro S hS; rw [(mem_powersetCard.1 hS).2]
    rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl hconst, Finset.sum_const, Finset.card_powersetCard, hn, smul_eq_mul]
  · intro c
    show F.coeff (Fintype.card {x // c x = true}) * G.coeff (Fintype.card {x // c x = false})
       = F.coeff ((boolFinset (Fin n) c).card) * G.coeff (n - (boolFinset (Fin n) c).card)
    have key : (univ.filter (fun x : Fin n => c x = false)).card
        = n - (univ.filter (fun x : Fin n => c x = true)).card := by
      have h := Finset.card_filter_add_card_filter_not (s := (univ : Finset (Fin n)))
        (fun x => c x = true)
      simp only [card_univ, Fintype.card_fin] at h
      have hff : (univ.filter (fun x : Fin n => ¬ c x = true))
          = univ.filter (fun x => c x = false) := by
        apply Finset.filter_congr; intro x _; simp [Bool.not_eq_true]
      rw [hff] at h; omega
    simp only [boolFinset, Equiv.coe_fn_mk]
    rw [Fintype.card_subtype, Fintype.card_subtype, key]

/-- **The central bridge theorem.**  The counting sequence of a product of species is the
*binomial convolution* of the factor sequences:
`(F ⊗ G).coeff n = ∑_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k) · F.coeff k · G.coeff (n-k)`.
Dividing by `n!`, this is exactly the Cauchy product of exponential generating functions
(see `SpeciesEGF.egfCoeff_prod`). -/
theorem coeff_prod (F G : Species) (n : ℕ) :
    (F.prod G).coeff n = ∑ k ∈ range (n+1), n.choose k * (F.coeff k * G.coeff (n-k)) := by
  have h := card_prod_obj F G (Fin n)
  rw [show (F.prod G).coeff n
      = @Fintype.card ((F.prod G).obj (Fin n)) ((F.prod G).finite (Fin n)) from rfl, h]
  exact coloring_sum_eq_binom F G n

/-! ### Two fundamental species -/

/-- The **species of sets** `E`: there is a unique `E`-structure on every set. -/
def E : Species where
  obj _ := Unit
  map _ := id
  map_id _ := rfl
  map_comp _ _ _ := rfl
  finite _ := inferInstance

/-- The species of sets counts `1` for every `n` (its EGF is `eˣ`). -/
theorem coeff_E (n : ℕ) : E.coeff n = 1 := by
  simp [coeff, E]

/-- The **species of permutations** `Perm`: a `Perm`-structure on `α` is a permutation of
`α`, transported by conjugation (`Equiv.permCongr`). -/
noncomputable def Perm : Species where
  obj α := Equiv.Perm α
  map e := Equiv.permCongr e
  map_id x := by simp
  map_comp e f x := by ext y; simp [Equiv.permCongr_apply]
  finite α := by classical exact inferInstance

/-- The species of permutations counts `n!` (its EGF is `1/(1-x)`). -/
theorem coeff_Perm (n : ℕ) : Perm.coeff n = n.factorial := by
  classical
  rw [coeff, show (Perm.finite (Fin n))
      = (inferInstance : Fintype (Equiv.Perm (Fin n))) from Subsingleton.elim _ _]
  change @Fintype.card (Equiv.Perm (Fin n)) _ = _
  rw [Fintype.card_perm, Fintype.card_fin]

end Species

open Finset

namespace Species

/-- The `n`-th coefficient of the exponential generating function of `F`, i.e.
`F.coeff n / n!`. -/
noncomputable def egfCoeff (F : Species) (n : ℕ) : ℝ := (F.coeff n : ℝ) / n.factorial

/-- The exponential generating function of `F` as a real power series `∑ aₙ xⁿ / n!`. -/
noncomputable def egf (F : Species) (x : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑' n : ℕ, (F.coeff n : ℝ) * x ^ n / n.factorial

/-- The EGF coefficients of a sum of species add. -/
theorem egfCoeff_sum (F G : Species) (n : ℕ) :
    (F.sum G).egfCoeff n = F.egfCoeff n + G.egfCoeff n := by
  unfold egfCoeff
  rw [coeff_sum]; push_cast; ring

/-- **The analytic bridge.**  The EGF coefficients of a product of species form the
*Cauchy product* of the factor EGFs:
`egfCoeff (F ⊗ G) n = ∑_{k=0}^{n} egfCoeff F k · egfCoeff G (n-k)`.
This is the exponential-generating-function form of `coeff_prod`: the analytic functor of
a species product multiplies generating functions. -/
theorem egfCoeff_prod (F G : Species) (n : ℕ) :
    (F.prod G).egfCoeff n = ∑ k ∈ range (n+1), F.egfCoeff k * G.egfCoeff (n-k) := by
  rw [egfCoeff, coeff_prod, Nat.cast_sum, Finset.sum_div]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro k hk
  rw [Finset.mem_range, Nat.lt_succ_iff] at hk
  rw [egfCoeff, egfCoeff]
  have hfac : (n.choose k : ℝ) * (k.factorial * (n-k).factorial) = n.factorial := by
    have h := Nat.choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial hk
    have h2 : ((n.choose k * k.factorial * (n-k).factorial : ℕ) : ℝ) = (n.factorial : ℝ) := by
      exact_mod_cast h
    push_cast at h2; linarith [h2]
  have hk0 : (k.factorial : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by positivity
  have hnk0 : ((n-k).factorial : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by positivity
  have hn0 : (n.factorial : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by positivity
  push_cast
  field_simp
  linear_combination (F.coeff k : ℝ) * (G.coeff (n-k) : ℝ) * hfac

/-- The exponential generating function of the species of sets is `eˣ`. -/
theorem egf_E (x : ℝ) : E.egf x = Real.exp x := by
  rw [egf, Real.exp_eq_exp_ℝ, NormedSpace.exp_eq_tsum_div]
  apply tsum_congr
  intro n
  rw [coeff_E]; push_cast; ring

/-- The EGF of the species of permutations is the geometric series `∑ xⁿ`. -/
theorem egf_Perm_eq_geom (x : ℝ) : Perm.egf x = ∑' n : ℕ, x ^ n := by
  rw [egf]; apply tsum_congr; intro n
  rw [coeff_Perm]
  have : (n.factorial : ℝ) ≠ 0 := by positivity
  field_simp

/-- The exponential generating function of the species of permutations is `1/(1-x)` for
`|x| < 1`. -/
theorem egf_Perm (x : ℝ) (hx : |x| < 1) : Perm.egf x = (1 - x)⁻¹ := by
  rw [egf_Perm_eq_geom]

itself counts `2ⁿ` (it assigns to an `n`-set the choices of a distinguished subset),

theorem coeff_E_prod_E (n : ℕ) : (E.prod E).coeff n = 2 ^ n := by
  rw [coeff_prod]
  simp only [coeff_E, mul_one]

    (h : FactorialNumberSystem.Valid c n) :
    FactorialNumberSystem.value c n < Perm.coeff n := by
  rw [coeff_Perm]
  exact FactorialNumberSystem.value_lt h

    ∃ c : ℕ → ℕ, FactorialNumberSystem.Valid c n ∧ FactorialNumberSystem.value c n = m := by
  rw [coeff_Perm] at hm
  exact ⟨FactorialNumberSystem.digit m, FactorialNumberSystem.digit_valid m n,
    FactorialNumberSystem.value_digit hm⟩

# Computational Evidence — Combinatorial Species and their EGFs

This note records the small-case calculations that guided the formalization in
`CombinatorialSpecies.lean` and `SpeciesEGF.lean`. All claims below are subsequently
proved in Lean (0 sorries); the tables are sanity checks, not the verification itself.

## 1. Counting sequences of the basic species

| species | `coeff 0` | `coeff 1` | `coeff 2` | `coeff 3` | `coeff 4` | EGF |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `E` (sets) | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | `eˣ` |
| `Perm` (permutations) | 1 | 1 | 2 | 6 | 24 | `1/(1-x)` |

`Perm.coeff n = n!` is OEIS **A000142** (factorials). `E.coeff n = 1` is the all-ones
sequence OEIS **A000012**.

## 2. The product bridge (binomial convolution)

For species `F, G`, the formalized identity is
`(F ⊗ G).coeff n = Σ_{k=0}^{n} C(n,k) · F.coeff k · G.coeff (n-k)`.

Check `E ⊗ E` (both sequences all-ones):

| n | `Σ_k C(n,k)·1·1` | closed form `2ⁿ` |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 1+1 = 2 | 2 |
| 2 | 1+2+1 = 4 | 4 |
| 3 | 1+3+3+1 = 8 | 8 |
| 4 | 1+4+6+4+1 = 16 | 16 |

So `(E ⊗ E).coeff n = 2ⁿ` (OEIS **A000079**), proved as `coeff_E_prod_E`.

Check `Perm ⊗ E` (a permutation on a chosen subset, nothing on the rest):
`Σ_k C(n,k)·k!·1 = Σ_k n!/(n-k)!` = number of partial permutations / arrangements,
OEIS **A000522**: 1, 2, 5, 16, 65, … (the EGF is `eˣ/(1-x)`). This matches the analytic
prediction `egf Perm · egf E = eˣ/(1-x)` from `egfCoeff_prod` + `egf_E` + `egf_Perm`.

## 3. The EGF (analytic functor) coefficients

`egfCoeff F n = F.coeff n / n!`. For `E`: `egfCoeff E n = 1/n!`, whose sum `Σ 1/n! · xⁿ`
is `eˣ` (proved as `egf_E`). For `Perm`: `egfCoeff Perm n = n!/n! = 1`, so the EGF is the
geometric series `Σ xⁿ = 1/(1-x)` (proved as `egf_Perm`, for `|x|<1`).

The product rule `egfCoeff (F ⊗ G) n = Σ_{k} egfCoeff F k · egfCoeff G (n-k)` is the
Cauchy product, verified per-degree from `C(n,k)/n! = 1/(k!(n-k)!)`.

## 4. Bridge to the factorial number system

`Perm.coeff n = n!` is exactly the number of valid length-`n` factoradic codes:
each integer `m < n!` has a unique factoradic representation. Small case `n = 3`
(`3! = 6`): the codes `(c₀,c₁,c₂)` with `cᵢ ≤ i` are
`(0,0,0)=0, (0,0,1)=2, (0,0,2)=4, (0,1,0)=1, (0,1,1)=3, (0,1,2)=5`, hitting `{0,…,5}`
bijectively. This is the content of `factoradic_lt_perm_count` and
`perm_index_has_factoradic`, reusing `FactorialNumberSystem` from the catalog.

## 5. Counterexample hunt

- "Is `(F ⊗ G).coeff` ever the ordinary (non-binomial) convolution?" — No: for `E ⊗ E`,
  ordinary convolution gives `Σ_k 1·1 = n+1`, but the true count is `2ⁿ`; they disagree
  from `n = 2` on. The binomial weights `C(n,k)` are essential (this is exactly why EGFs,
  not ordinary GFs, are the right transform for labelled structures).
- "Does counting depend on the chosen labelling of the `n`-set?" — No, by transport
  invariance `card_obj`; tested implicitly since `coeff` is defined via `Fin n` and the
  proofs hold for arbitrary finite `α`.

# Future Directions: Species, Functors, and Analytic Combinatorics

This cycle established the functorial foundations of combinatorial species over finite
sets and proved the first half of Joyal's dictionary: the *sum* of species adds counting
sequences, and the *product* of species realizes the binomial convolution, which on the
exponential-generating-function side is exactly the Cauchy product. The species of sets
and of permutations were realized concretely, with their generating functions identified
as the exponential and the geometric series. The following conjectures extend this
program toward a complete, machine-checkable theory of analytic functors.

## 1. The composition of species is functional substitution of generating functions

**Conjecture.** For species `F` and `G` with `G` having no structure on the empty set,
the counting sequence of the composite `F ∘ G` (partition the underlying set into nonempty
blocks, place a `G`-structure on each block and an `F`-structure on the set of blocks)
has exponential generating function equal to the substitution `EGF_F(EGF_G(x))`.

The key insight is that the binomial convolution already proved for products is the
"two-block" shadow of a general multinomial sum over set partitions, so composition is the
unique operation making generating functions close under substitution. Why now? The
product bridge supplies the exact algebraic identity (`C(n,k)/n! = 1/(k!(n-k)!)`) whose
multinomial generalization is the only missing ingredient; the functorial transport
machinery for blocks is already in place via the coloring/partition encoding.

## 2. Every polynomial functor is the analytic functor of a unique species

**Conjecture.** A functor on finite sets is *analytic* (a possibly infinite sum of
representables weighted by symmetric-group actions) if and only if it arises as the
structure functor of a species, and the species is determined up to isomorphism by the
sequence of cardinalities of its structures together with the induced permutation actions.

The key insight is that transport invariance (`card_obj`) already collapses a species to a
sequence of finite sets carrying symmetric-group actions, so the classification reduces to
recognizing which functors factor through this groupoid data. Why now? With species
formalized as honest functors sending bijections to bijections, the representability
criterion can be tested directly against the two extremal examples (`E` and `Perm`) that
this cycle constructed.

## 3. The derivative of a species differentiates its generating function

**Conjecture.** The species derivative `F′` (an `F′`-structure on a set is an `F`-structure
on that set augmented by one new distinguished point) satisfies
`(F′).coeff n = F.coeff (n+1)`, and hence its exponential generating function is the formal
derivative of that of `F`.

The key insight is that adjoining a ghost point is a bijection-respecting reindexing by
one, so the counting recurrence is forced and the `1/n!` weighting turns the index shift
into termwise differentiation. Why now? The transport-invariance lemma makes the
"add a point" operation manifestly functorial, and the EGF-coefficient calculus developed
here (`egfCoeff`) already isolates exactly the `xⁿ/n!` bookkeeping that differentiation
acts on.

## 4. The factorial number system is the canonical linear order on permutation labels

**Conjecture.** The bijection between integers below `n!` and length-`n` factoradic codes
extends to a natural isomorphism between the species of permutations and the species of
linear orders, under which the factoradic value computes the Lehmer code (the inversion
table) of a permutation.

The key insight is that both species have counting sequence `n!`, and the factorial number
system is precisely the mixed-radix readout of inversion counts, so the abstract
"same generating function" coincidence is witnessed by an explicit, computable map. Why
now? This cycle already connected the permutation count to the factorial number system
(`factoradic_lt_perm_count`, `perm_index_has_factoradic`); upgrading the numerical
coincidence to a natural isomorphism of functors is the natural next step.

## 5. Labelled and unlabelled enumeration are reconciled by averaging over symmetry

**Conjecture.** For any species `F`, the unlabelled count (isomorphism classes of
`F`-structures on an `n`-set) equals the average of fixed-point counts of the induced
symmetric-group action, and the ordinary generating function of unlabelled structures is
obtained from the cycle-index series by a single specialization.

The key insight is that the same functorial transport that makes labelled counting
well-defined also generates a group action whose orbit count, by Burnside's lemma, is the
unlabelled count — so labelled and unlabelled enumeration are two evaluations of one
functor. Why now? Species are now formalized as functors carrying exactly these symmetry
actions, so the orbit-counting bridge can be stated and attacked without any further
infrastructure.

concept.concept_description: Formalize two concrete degree-counting theorems about Airy's equation y'' = x·y in the polynomial ring ℝ[X], using Mathlib's Polynomial API with formal derivative. Theorem 1 (Polynomial obstruction): There is no nonzero polynomial p such that p'' = X · p in ℝ[X]. """Numerical demonstrations for the nonexistence of polynomial solutions to
Airy's equation y'' = x*y and its Riccati form u' + u^2 = x.

The two theorems established are:

    Theorem A (linear form).   The only polynomial p with p'' = x*p is p = 0.
    Theorem B (Riccati form).  No polynomial u satisfies u' + u^2 = x.

This script represents polynomials by their coefficient lists and implements
the formal derivative, multiplication by x, and degree, so that the
degree-counting arguments behind both theorems can be exhibited explicitly and
checked on concrete examples. Everything is self-contained: no third-party
libraries are required.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List

# A polynomial is represented as a list of real coefficients in ascending
# order of degree:  [a0, a1, a2, ...]  denotes  a0 + a1*x + a2*x^2 + ...


def trim(p: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Remove trailing (high-degree) zero coefficients; [] denotes the zero poly."""
    q = list(p)
    while q and abs(q[-1]) < 1e-12:
        q.pop()
    return q


def degree(p: List[float]) -> int:
    """Degree of a polynomial; the zero polynomial is given degree -1."""
    q = trim(p)
    return len(q) - 1


def derivative(p: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Formal derivative:  d/dx sum a_k x^k = sum k a_k x^{k-1}."""
    q = trim(p)
    if len(q) <= 1:
        return []
    return trim([k * q[k] for k in range(1, len(q))])


def mul_by_x(p: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Multiply a polynomial by x: shift all coefficients up by one degree."""
    q = trim(p)
    if not q:
        return []
    return [0.0] + q


def add(p: List[float], q: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Add two polynomials."""
    n = max(len(p), len(q))
    pe = p + [0.0] * (n - len(p))
    qe = q + [0.0] * (n - len(q))
    return trim([pe[i] + qe[i] for i in range(n)])


def mul(p: List[float], q: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Multiply two polynomials (convolution of coefficient lists)."""
    p, q = trim(p), trim(q)
    if not p or not q:
        return []
    out = [0.0] * (len(p) + len(q) - 1)
    for i, a in enumerate(p):
        for j, b in enumerate(q):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return trim(out)


def square(p: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Square a polynomial."""
    return mul(p, p)


def fmt(p: List[float]) -> str:
    """Pretty-print a polynomial."""
    q = trim(p)
    if not q:
        return "0"
    terms = []
    for k, a in enumerate(q):
        if abs(a) < 1e-12:
            continue
        if k == 0:
            terms.append(f"{a:g}")
        elif k == 1:
            terms.append(f"{a:g}*x")
        else:
            terms.append(f"{a:g}*x^{k}")
    return " + ".join(terms) if terms else "0"

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

    """Return p'' - x*p; this is zero exactly when p solves Airy's equation."""
    return add(derivative(derivative(p)), [-c for c in mul_by_x(p)])

    print("   deg(x*p)  = n + 1   (multiplication by x raises degree by 1)")
    print("   deg(p'')  <= n - 2  (each derivative lowers degree by >= 1)")
    print("These can never be equal, so no nonzero polynomial can solve it.\n")

    test_polys = {
        "1 (constant)":      [1.0],
        "x":                 [0.0, 1.0],
        "x^2":               [0.0, 0.0, 1.0],
        "3x^4 - x + 7":      [7.0, -1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 3.0],

# Demonstration 2: the Riccati form u' + u^2 = x.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def riccati_residual(u: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Return u' + u^2 - x; zero exactly when u solves the Riccati equation."""
    return add(add(derivative(u), square(u)), [0.0, -1.0])


def demo_riccati() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Demonstration 2: Riccati form  u' + u^2 = x")

    print("   deg(u^2) = 2d,   deg(u') <= d - 1,   deg(x) = 1.")

    print("   d >= 1: u^2 dominates, LHS has degree 2d >= 2 != 1.")
    print("So no polynomial u can solve it -- not even u = 0.\n")

        "1":             [1.0],
        "x":             [0.0, 1.0],

        "x^2":           [0.0, 0.0, 1.0],

    for name, u in test_polys.items():
        d = degree(u)
        d_sq = degree(square(u))
        d_du = degree(derivative(u))
        res = riccati_residual(u)
        print(f"  u = {name}")
        print(f"     deg u = {d},  deg(u^2) = {d_sq},  deg(u') = {d_du}")
        print(f"     residual u' + u^2 - x = {fmt(res)}  (never zero)")
    print()

def demo_general_coefficient() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Demonstration 3: generalized form  p'' = q*p,  deg q >= 1")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Same degree gap: deg(q*p) = deg q + n >= n + 1 > n - 2 >= deg(p'').")
    print("So p'' = q*p has only the zero polynomial solution for any such q.\n")

    q_list = {
        "q = x":          [0.0, 1.0],
        "q = x^2 + 1":    [1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
        "q = 2x^3":       [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 2.0],

        rhs = mul(q, p)
        residual = add(lhs, [-c for c in rhs])
        print(f"  {name},  p = 3x^4 - x + 7")
        print(f"     deg(q*p) = {degree(rhs)},  deg(p'') = {degree(lhs)}")
        print(f"     residual p'' - q*p = {fmt(residual)}  (nonzero)\n")

# Demonstration 4: contrast with the convergent power-series solution.
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

def airy_series_coeffs(num_terms: int) -> List[float]:
    """Coefficients a_k of a power-series solution of y'' = x*y with a_0 = 1,
    a_1 = 0, obtained from the recurrence (k+2)(k+1) a_{k+2} = a_{k-1}.

    This shows the solution exists as an *infinite* series with infinitely many
    nonzero coefficients -- precisely why it is not a polynomial.
    """
    a = [0.0] * num_terms
    if num_terms > 0:
        a[0] = 1.0
    if num_terms > 1:
        a[1] = 0.0
    for k in range(num_terms - 2):
        prev = a[k - 1] if k - 1 >= 0 else 0.0
        a[k + 2] = prev / ((k + 2) * (k + 1))
    return a


def demo_power_series() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Demonstration 4: the genuine (non-polynomial) series solution")
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Airy's equation DOES have a power-series solution, but it has")
    print("infinitely many nonzero coefficients -- it is not a polynomial.\n")
    coeffs = airy_series_coeffs(13)
    nonzero = [(k, c) for k, c in enumerate(coeffs) if abs(c) > 1e-12]
    print("  Nonzero coefficients a_k (a_0 = 1, a_1 = 0):")
    for k, c in nonzero:
        print(f"     a_{k:<2} = {c:.10f}")
    print("\n  The pattern a_{3m} = 1 / [ (2)(3)(5)(6)...(3m-1)(3m) ] continues")
    print("  forever: there is no highest degree, hence no polynomial.\n")


def main() -> None:
    demo_linear_degree_gap()
    demo_riccati()
    demo_general_coefficient()
    demo_power_series()
    print("=" * 70)
    print("Summary: degree counting forbids polynomial solutions of both the")
    print("linear and Riccati forms of Airy's equation; the true solution is")
    print("an irreducibly infinite power series.")
    print("=" * 70)

    main()

# Computational Evidence — Airy's Equation Has No EML Solutions

This note collects the small-case evidence that motivated the formal theorems in
`AiryNoEMLSolution.lean` and `RiccatiBoundary.lean`.

## 1. Polynomial solutions of `y'' = x·y`

Write `p = Σ aₙ xⁿ`. Then `p''` has degree `deg p − 2`, while `x·p` has degree
`deg p + 1`. Matching the top coefficient is impossible for any `p ≠ 0`:

| `deg p` | `deg p''` | `deg (x·p)` | match? |
|--------:|----------:|------------:|:------:|
| 0       | (−∞)      | 1           | no     |
| 1       | (−∞)      | 2           | no     |
| 2       | 0         | 3           | no     |
| `n`     | `n−2`     | `n+1`       | no     |

The gap `( n+1 ) − ( n−2 ) = 3` never closes, so the only polynomial solution is `p = 0`.
(Formalized as `airy_no_polynomial_solution`.)

## 2. Exp-of-polynomial solutions `y = exp(p)`

Substituting `y = exp(p)` into `y'' = x·y` and dividing by `exp(p) > 0` gives the Riccati
relation
```
(p')² + p'' = x.
```
Let `q = p'` with `deg q = d`.

| case        | `deg (q²)` | `deg q'` | `deg` of LHS | target `deg x` = 1 |
|-------------|-----------:|---------:|-------------:|:------------------:|
| `q = 0`     | (−∞)       | (−∞)     | `−∞` (LHS=0) | no (0 ≠ x)         |
| `d = 0`     | 0          | (−∞)     | 0            | no                 |
| `d ≥ 1`     | `2d`       | `≤ d−1`  | `2d` (even)  | no (`2d ≠ 1`)      |

The left-hand side always has **even** degree (or is constant), never degree 1.
(Formalized as `airy_riccati_no_polynomial_solution`.)

### Explicit small checks
* `p = a + b·x`  ⇒ `(p')² + p'' = b²` (constant) ≠ `x`.
* `p = c·x²`     ⇒ `p' = 2c·x`, `(p')² = 4c²x²`, `p'' = 2c`, sum `= 4c²x² + 2c` ≠ `x`.
* `p = c·x²/2`   ⇒ same shape, leading term `c²x²` cannot be `x`.

No truncation up to degree 6 yields a solution; the parity obstruction rules out all degrees.

## 3. The degree-parity generalization

The same count shows `(p')² + p'' = r` is unsolvable whenever `deg r` is **odd**:
the LHS is always even-degree or constant. Airy is the smallest instance (`r = x`,
`deg = 1`). Predictions: `y'' = x³ y`, `y'' = (x⁵+1) y`, … all lack exp-of-polynomial
solutions. (Formalized as `riccati_no_solution_of_odd_natDegree`.)

## 4. The contrasting solvable case (boundary)

For a **constant** coefficient `k ≥ 0`, the Riccati relation becomes `(p')² + p'' = k`,
solved by `p = √k·x` (then `(p')² = (√k)² = k`, `p'' = 0`). The corresponding ODE
`y'' = k·y` has the genuine EML solution `y = exp(√k·x)`:
```
y'  = √k · exp(√k·x),     y'' = (√k)² · exp(√k·x) = k · exp(√k·x) = k·y.
```
(Formalized as `riccati_const_has_poly_solution` and `exp_solution_const_coeff`.)

## Summary

The decisive invariant is the **parity of the degree of the coefficient function**. Airy's
`x` has odd degree 1, which can never equal the even-degree square `(p')²`; constant
coefficients have even degree 0 and are solvable. This is precisely the obstruction that the
Kovacic algorithm detects in its exponential (Case 1) branch.

# Why Airy's Equation Refuses to Be a Polynomial

## A curve that bends the rules

In 1838 the British astronomer George Biddell Airy was trying to understand
a stubborn optical puzzle: what exactly happens to light near a *caustic*, the
bright fold you see at the edge of a rainbow or shimmering on the bottom of a
coffee cup? The wave theory of light told him that the brightness should be
governed by a single, deceptively simple differential equation:

$$ y'' = x\,y. $$

In words: the curvature of the function $y$ at each point $x$ is equal to the
function's own value, multiplied by how far you are from the origin. To the
left of zero the equation behaves like the equation of a spring, producing
gentle oscillations; to the right of zero it behaves like a runaway
exponential. Right at the origin the two regimes meet, and the resulting
function — the **Airy function** — sits at the heart of optics, quantum
mechanics, and the theory of random matrices.

Airy's equation looks like it ought to be tame. After all, its right-hand side
is just "$x$ times $y$" — about as simple as a variable coefficient can be. So
here is a natural question, the kind a curious student might ask on first
meeting the equation:

> Is there a *polynomial* that solves Airy's equation?

A polynomial — something like $p(x) = 3x^4 - x + 7$ — is the friendliest kind
of function there is. It is built from a finite number of powers of $x$, it is
infinitely smooth, and we can differentiate it forever without leaving the
world of polynomials. Many famous differential equations have beautiful
polynomial solutions: Legendre's equation gives the Legendre polynomials,
Hermite's equation gives the Hermite polynomials, and so on. Could Airy's
equation hide a polynomial too?

The answer, it turns out, is a clean and total **no** — and the reason why is
a small gem of mathematical reasoning that requires nothing more than counting.

## Counting the degree

Every nonzero polynomial has a **degree**: the highest power of $x$ that
appears in it. The polynomial $3x^4 - x + 7$ has degree $4$; the constant $5$
has degree $0$. The degree is a kind of fingerprint, and it interacts with the
basic operations of algebra in completely predictable ways.

Two rules are all we need.

**Rule 1 — Multiplying by $x$ raises the degree by one.** If $p$ has degree
$n$, then $x \cdot p$ has degree $n+1$. Multiplying by $x$ shifts every term up
one power, so the top term $x^n$ becomes $x^{n+1}$. Nothing can cancel it.

**Rule 2 — Differentiating lowers the degree by (at least) one.** The
derivative of $x^n$ is $n\,x^{n-1}$, so taking a derivative knocks the degree
down by one. Differentiate *twice* and you lose at least two degrees: the
second derivative $p''$ has degree at most $n - 2$.

Now put the two sides of Airy's equation head to head. Suppose, for the sake of
argument, that some nonzero polynomial $p$ of degree $n$ satisfied $p'' = x\,p$.

* The **right-hand side**, $x \cdot p$, has degree $n + 1$ by Rule 1.
* The **left-hand side**, $p''$, has degree at most $n - 2$ by Rule 2.

But if two polynomials are equal, they must have the *same* degree. We would
need
$$ n + 1 \le n - 2, $$
which simplifies to $1 \le -2$. That is absurd. The right-hand side is always
*more* wiggly — higher degree — than the left-hand side can ever be. There is
no room for the two to meet.

The only escape hatch is the polynomial we quietly excluded at the start: the
**zero polynomial**, $p = 0$, which has no degree to compare and trivially
satisfies $0 = x \cdot 0$. And that is the whole story.

> **Theorem (No polynomial solutions of Airy's equation).** The only
> polynomial $p$ satisfying $p'' = x\,p$ is the zero polynomial $p = 0$.

What is striking is how little machinery the proof needs. No calculus of
limits, no infinite series, no clever substitution — just the observation that
multiplying by $x$ pushes a polynomial *up* the degree ladder while
differentiating pulls it *down*, and the two can never be reconciled.

## A second disguise: the Riccati form

Differential equations love disguises. A standard trick for studying a
second-order linear equation like Airy's is to look not at $y$ itself but at
the **logarithmic derivative** $u = y'/y$ — the relative rate at which $y$ is
growing. This substitution turns the linear equation into a *nonlinear* one
called a **Riccati equation**. For Airy's equation, the logarithmic-derivative
substitution produces

$$ u' + u^2 = x. $$

This is the same equation wearing a different costume. It is natural to ask the
same question of it: does the Riccati form admit a polynomial solution $u$? And
again the answer is a flat **no** — but now the degree-counting argument has a
small twist, because of that squared term $u^2$.

Suppose $u$ is a polynomial of degree $d$. We compare the degrees of the three
pieces.

* The term $u^2$ has degree $2d$, because squaring a polynomial doubles its
  degree.
* The term $u'$ has degree at most $d - 1$, one less than $u$.
* The right-hand side $x$ has degree exactly $1$.

Now split into two cases.

**Case 1: $u$ is a constant ($d = 0$).** Then $u'$ is zero and $u^2$ is a
constant, so the entire left-hand side $u' + u^2$ is a constant — degree $0$.
But the right-hand side $x$ has degree $1$. A constant can never equal $x$.
Contradiction.

**Case 2: $u$ has degree $d \ge 1$.** Now the squared term dominates
everything. Its degree $2d$ is at least $2$, and it strictly exceeds the degree
of $u'$ (which is at most $d-1 < 2d$). When you add a high-degree polynomial to
a strictly lower-degree one, the high degree survives — nothing cancels the top
term. So $u' + u^2$ has degree exactly $2d \ge 2$. But the right-hand side $x$
has degree $1$. Again the degrees cannot match.

Either way we reach a contradiction, and so:

> **Theorem (No polynomial solutions of the Riccati form).** There is no
> polynomial $u$ satisfying $u' + u^2 = x$.

Here there is not even a zero-polynomial escape hatch: the Riccati equation has
*no* polynomial solution whatsoever, not even the trivial one, because $0' +
0^2 = 0 \ne x$.

## Why this matters

It would be easy to dismiss these results as negative trivia — "this equation
doesn't have *that* kind of solution, so what?" But absence theorems are some
of the most useful tools in mathematics, precisely because they tell you where
*not* to look.

The Airy function genuinely exists; it is smooth, well-behaved, and central to
physics. What our two theorems prove is that this function lives *outside* the
cozy world of polynomials. No amount of algebraic cleverness — no finite
combination of powers of $x$ — will ever capture it. To write the Airy function
down you are forced into richer territory: infinite power series, integrals,
or special transcendental functions. The simplicity of the equation is a kind
of trap; its solutions are irreducibly more complicated than the equation that
defines them.

This is a recurring theme across mathematics and physics. The pendulum's exact
period cannot be written with elementary functions. The orbit of three
gravitating bodies has no closed-form solution. Time and again, a short,
innocent-looking equation turns out to demand answers that no finite formula
can express. The degree-counting proof for Airy's equation is a miniature,
fully rigorous instance of this phenomenon — and one you can verify with pencil
and paper in a single sitting.

## The shape of the argument

Step back and notice the architecture of both proofs, because the same skeleton
appears throughout the study of differential equations with polynomial
coefficients.

1. **Assume a polynomial solution exists**, and give its degree a name.
2. **Track how each operation moves the degree.** Multiplication by $x$ adds
   one; differentiation subtracts (at least) one; squaring doubles.
3. **Compare the two sides of the equation.** If they are forced to have
   different degrees, no such solution can exist.

This "degree bookkeeping" is a complete, self-contained method. It generalizes
immediately. Replace $x$ by any polynomial coefficient $q(x)$ of degree at
least one, and the equation $p'' = q\,p$ still has no nonzero polynomial
solution, by exactly the same imbalance: the right-hand side outpaces the left.
Push to higher derivatives, $p^{(k)} = x\,p$, and the gap only widens. The
single idea — *that some operations build polynomials up faster than others can
tear them down* — rules out an entire family of would-be solutions in one
stroke.

Airy set out to explain a band of light at the edge of a rainbow. Two hundred
years later, the equation he wrote down still rewards a fresh look — and one of
its secrets, that it can never be solved by a polynomial, turns out to rest on
nothing deeper than knowing how to count.

# Nonexistence of Polynomial Solutions for Airy's Equation and Its Riccati Form

## Abstract

We prove two sharp nonexistence results concerning Airy's differential
equation, the classical second-order linear equation $y'' = x\,y$ that governs
wave amplitudes near a caustic. Working purely algebraically in the polynomial
ring $\mathbb{R}[x]$ equipped with the formal derivative, we show that the only
polynomial $p$ satisfying $p'' = x\,p$ is the zero polynomial, and that the
associated Riccati equation $u' + u^2 = x$ — obtained from the logarithmic
derivative substitution — has no polynomial solution at all. Both proofs are
elementary degree-counting arguments, requiring no analysis, no convergence
considerations, and no real-valued functions: they rest only on the additivity
of degree under multiplication, the strict degree drop under differentiation,
and the dominance of a strictly higher-degree summand. We isolate the structural
core of these arguments, explain why they generalize to equations of the form
$p'' = q\,p$ for any coefficient $q$ of positive degree and to higher-order
analogues $p^{(k)} = x\,p$, and discuss the consequences for the
transcendence of the Airy function and for the differential algebra of
equations with polynomial coefficients.

## 1. Introduction

Airy's equation
$$ y'' = x\,y \tag{1} $$
arose in George Biddell Airy's 1838 study of the intensity of light near a
caustic. It is the simplest second-order linear ordinary differential equation
whose coefficient varies linearly with the independent variable, and as such it
sits at a boundary: for $x < 0$ its solutions oscillate, while for $x > 0$ they
behave exponentially. Its solutions, the Airy functions $\operatorname{Ai}(x)$
and $\operatorname{Bi}(x)$, are ubiquitous in optics, semiclassical quantum
mechanics (the connection problem at a turning point), the asymptotics of
orthogonal polynomials, and the Tracy–Widom laws of random matrix theory.

Despite the analytic richness of its solutions, equation (1) has a coefficient,
$x$, that is itself a polynomial. It is therefore natural to ask whether (1)
admits solutions within the simplest possible function class — the polynomials.
Many classical equations do: Legendre's, Hermite's, Laguerre's, and Chebyshev's
equations all possess polynomial eigensolutions. The purpose of this paper is to
establish, with complete rigor and by entirely elementary means, that Airy's
equation does **not**.

We prove two results.

1. **(Linear form.)** The only $p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ with $p'' = x\,p$ is
   $p = 0$.
2. **(Riccati form.)** No $p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ satisfies $p'' + (p')^2 = x$.

The Riccati form is the equation satisfied by the antiderivative of a
logarithmic derivative of a solution of (1); we elaborate on this connection in
Section 5. Both proofs are degree-counting arguments carried out in the formal
polynomial ring, so they make no reference to limits, convergence, or
real-analytic structure. This algebraic stance is what makes the results both
sharp and effortlessly generalizable.

## 2. Preliminaries: the degree calculus

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}[x]$ denotes the ring of polynomials in one indeterminate
$x$ over the real numbers, and for a polynomial $p$ we write $p'$ for its
**formal derivative**, defined termwise by $\frac{d}{dx} x^n = n\,x^{n-1}$ and
extended linearly. The formal derivative satisfies the usual product and power
rules purely algebraically.

For a nonzero polynomial $p$, $\deg p$ denotes its **degree**, the largest $n$
with a nonzero coefficient of $x^n$. We adopt the convention used throughout
that for the **natural-number degree** $\operatorname{natDeg}$ one has
$\operatorname{natDeg} 0 = 0$, with the understanding that the zero polynomial
is handled separately whenever degree comparisons are made. All inequalities
below involving truncated subtraction on $\mathbb{N}$ are interpreted in the
natural numbers (so $a - b = 0$ when $b \ge a$); this matches the way the proofs
manipulate degrees and is harmless because the cases that matter have $a \ge b$.

We record the three facts that drive every argument in this paper.

**Lemma 2.1 (Degree of a product with $x$).** For any nonzero $p \in
\mathbb{R}[x]$,
$$ \deg(x\,p) = \deg p + 1. $$

*Proof.* Multiplication by $x$ sends $\sum_k a_k x^k$ to $\sum_k a_k x^{k+1}$.
If $a_n$ is the leading coefficient of $p$ (so $a_n \ne 0$ and $n = \deg p$),
then $a_n x^{n+1}$ is the leading term of $x\,p$, and it does not vanish because
$\mathbb{R}$ has no zero divisors. Hence $\deg(x\,p) = n + 1$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2.2 (Degree drop under differentiation).** For any $p \in
\mathbb{R}[x]$,
$$ \deg(p') \le \deg p - 1, $$
and consequently $\deg(p'') \le \deg p - 2$.

*Proof.* Differentiating $\sum_k a_k x^k$ gives $\sum_k k\,a_k x^{k-1}$, every
term of which has degree strictly less than the corresponding term of $p$. Thus
$\deg(p') \le \deg p - 1$. Applying the bound twice gives $\deg(p'') \le
(\deg p - 1) - 1 = \deg p - 2$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2.3 (Dominance of a strictly larger summand).** If $a, b \in
\mathbb{R}[x]$ satisfy $\deg a < \deg b$, then
$$ \deg(a + b) = \deg b. $$

*Proof.* The coefficient of $x^{\deg b}$ in $a + b$ equals the leading
coefficient of $b$ (since $a$ contributes nothing in that degree), which is
nonzero, and no higher-degree term appears. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Lemma 2.4 (Degree of a square).** For any $p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$,
$$ \deg(p^2) = 2 \deg p. $$

*Proof.* The leading term of $p^2$ is the square of the leading term of $p$,
whose coefficient is the square of a nonzero real and hence nonzero. $\qquad\blacksquare$

These four lemmas are the entire toolbox.

## 3. The linear form

**Theorem 3.1 (No nonzero polynomial solution of Airy's equation).** Let $p \in
\mathbb{R}[x]$ satisfy
$$ p'' = x\,p. \tag{2} $$
Then $p = 0$.

*Proof.* Suppose for contradiction that $p \ne 0$, and set $n = \deg p$.

Comparing the two sides of (2) as equal polynomials, they must have equal
degree. By Lemma 2.1, the right-hand side satisfies
$$ \deg(x\,p) = n + 1. $$
By Lemma 2.2, the left-hand side satisfies
$$ \deg(p'') \le n - 2. $$
Since $p'' = x\,p$, these two quantities are the same number, so
$$ n + 1 = \deg(p'') \le n - 2, $$
whence $n + 1 \le n - 2$, i.e. $3 \le 0$, a contradiction. Therefore $p = 0$.
Conversely $p = 0$ does satisfy (2), since $0 = x \cdot 0$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

The proof exposes the mechanism precisely: multiplication by $x$ raises the
degree by one, while two differentiations lower it by two, creating a permanent
gap of three between the two sides. No polynomial can bridge a gap that the
equation itself forces open.

## 4. The Riccati form

We now turn to the nonlinear companion equation
$$ p'' + (p')^2 = x. \tag{3} $$
Equation (3) is the equation satisfied by an antiderivative of a logarithmic
derivative of a solution of (1); see Section 5. Whereas the linear form admits
the trivial solution $p = 0$, the Riccati form admits none at all.

**Theorem 4.1 (No polynomial solution of the Riccati form).** There is no
$p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ satisfying $p'' + (p')^2 = x$.

*Proof.* Suppose such a $p$ exists. Write $q = p'$ and let $d = \deg q$ (the
natural-number degree, so $d = 0$ when $q$ is constant). By Lemma 2.4,
$$ \deg(q^2) = 2d, $$
and by Lemma 2.2 applied to $q = p'$,
$$ \deg(p'') = \deg(q') \le d - 1. $$
We consider two cases according to the value of $d$.

**Case $d = 0$.** Then $q$ is a constant, so $q' = p'' = 0$ and $q^2$ is a
constant; thus the left-hand side $p'' + q^2$ is a constant, of degree $\le 0$.
By the degree-of-a-sum bound,
$$ \deg\bigl(p'' + (p')^2\bigr) \le \max\{\deg(p''),\, \deg(q^2)\} \le 0. $$
But equation (3) asserts this equals $\deg(x) = 1$, so $1 \le 0$, a
contradiction.

**Case $d \ge 1$.** Then $\deg(q^2) = 2d \ge 2$, while $\deg(p'') \le d - 1 <
2d$. The two summands therefore have strictly different degrees, and by Lemma
2.3 the larger one dominates:
$$ \deg\bigl(p'' + (p')^2\bigr) = \deg(q^2) = 2d. $$
Equation (3) forces this to equal $\deg(x) = 1$, so $2d = 1$ with $d \ge 1$, a
contradiction (and indeed $2d \ge 2 > 1$ already suffices).

In both cases we reach a contradiction, so no polynomial $p$ satisfies (3).
$\qquad\blacksquare$

The asymmetry between Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 is worth emphasizing. The linear
equation is homogeneous, so $p = 0$ is automatically a solution and the theorem
is a uniqueness statement (the *only* solution is zero). The Riccati equation is
inhomogeneous — its right-hand side is the nonzero polynomial $x$ — so even the
zero polynomial fails, and the conclusion is outright nonexistence.

The two theorems are not independent curiosities; the Riccati equation is the
standard nonlinear shadow of the linear one. Given a (sufficiently smooth,
locally nonvanishing) solution $y$ of $y'' = x\,y$, introduce the logarithmic
derivative
$$ w = \frac{y'}{y}. $$
Then $w' = \frac{y''}{y} - \left(\frac{y'}{y}\right)^2 = x - w^2$, i.e.
$$ w' + w^2 = x. \tag{4} $$
Equation (4) is the **Riccati form** of Airy's equation in the variable $w$.
Writing $w = p'$ for an antiderivative $p$ recasts (4) as (3). Thus a polynomial
solution of the Riccati form would correspond to a solution of Airy's equation
whose logarithmic derivative is a polynomial — the kind of "elementary" closed
form one might hope for. Theorem 4.1 shows no such closed form exists at the
level of polynomials, reinforcing Theorem 3.1 from the nonlinear side.

It bears stressing that Theorems 3.1 and 4.1 are proved entirely within the
formal polynomial ring; the analytic substitution above is given only to explain
*why* the Riccati form is the natural object to study. The proofs themselves
never leave algebra.

## 6. Generalizations

The degree calculus of Section 2 is robust, and both theorems generalize with no
new ideas.

**Theorem 6.1 (Polynomial coefficient of positive degree).** Let $q \in
\mathbb{R}[x]$ be a fixed nonzero polynomial with $\deg q \ge 1$. Then the only
$p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ satisfying $p'' = q\,p$ is $p = 0$.

*Sketch.* If $p \ne 0$ with $\deg p = n$, then $\deg(q\,p) = \deg q + n \ge n +
1$ by additivity of degree over the domain $\mathbb{R}[x]$, while $\deg(p'') \le
n - 2$. The inequality $n + 1 \le \deg q + n = \deg(p'') \le n - 2$ is again
impossible. Airy's equation is the case $q = x$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Theorem 6.2 (Higher-order analogue).** For any integer $k \ge 1$, the only
$p \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ satisfying $p^{(k)} = x\,p$ is $p = 0$.

*Sketch.* The $k$-th derivative obeys $\deg(p^{(k)}) \le n - k$, while
$\deg(x\,p) = n + 1$. Since $n + 1 > n - k$ for every $k \ge 0$, the degrees can
never match unless $p = 0$. $\qquad\blacksquare$

**Arbitrary base ring.** Lemmas 2.1, 2.3, and 2.4 use only that the coefficient
ring is a nontrivial commutative ring without zero divisors — an integral
domain — so that the leading coefficient of a product is the product of the
leading coefficients and hence nonzero. Consequently Theorems 3.1, 4.1, 6.1, and
6.2 hold verbatim over any integral domain $R$ in place of $\mathbb{R}$, e.g.
$\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{C}$, or a polynomial ring over a field. The
real numbers play no special role.

## 7. Discussion and consequences

**Transcendence of the Airy function.** Theorem 3.1 is the first rung on the
ladder of statements asserting that the Airy function is not "elementary."
Because the homogeneous solution space of (1) is two-dimensional and contains no
nonzero polynomial, every nonzero solution — in particular $\operatorname{Ai}$
and $\operatorname{Bi}$ — must be genuinely transcendental over the polynomials.
The Airy function does possess an everywhere-convergent power series and an
integral representation $\operatorname{Ai}(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\infty
\cos\!\left(\frac{t^3}{3} + xt\right)\,dt$, but it cannot be truncated to, or
captured by, any finite polynomial expression.

**The value of negative results.** Nonexistence theorems function as
*signposts*: they tell solvers and algorithm designers which ansätze are futile.
A symbolic ODE solver searching for polynomial solutions of (1) can terminate
immediately with the certificate provided by Theorem 3.1, and a search for a
polynomial logarithmic derivative can be pruned by Theorem 4.1. Degree-counting
certificates of this kind are cheap to check and, as Section 6 shows, easy to
extend to whole families of equations.

**Methodological remark.** The proofs deliberately avoid analysis. By
formulating Airy's equation in the formal polynomial ring with the formal
derivative, the statement "Airy's equation has no polynomial solution" becomes a
finite combinatorial fact about degrees, fully decidable by inspection of two
integers. This is a recurring advantage of the algebraic viewpoint on
differential equations: questions that look analytic become questions about the
degree, valuation, or factorization structure of polynomials.

## 8. Future work

Several natural directions remain.

* **Coefficients of arbitrary positive degree.** Theorem 6.1 generalizes the
  linear form to $p'' = q\,p$ for any nonzero $q$ with $\deg q \ge 1$; a fuller
  treatment would characterize exactly which polynomial coefficients $q$ (now
  allowing $\deg q = 0$, where Hermite-type polynomial solutions reappear) admit
  nonzero polynomial solutions, recovering the classical orthogonal-polynomial
  families as the boundary case.
* **General base rings.** Restating all results over an arbitrary integral
  domain $R$, or more weakly over a nontrivial commutative ring with no zero
  divisors, would maximize reusability and clarify exactly which ring-theoretic
  hypotheses the degree calculus requires.
* **Higher-order and mixed analogues.** Beyond $p^{(k)} = x\,p$, one can study
  Riccati-type identities mixing several derivatives, where the same comparison
  (left-hand degree $\le n - k$, right-hand degree $n + 1$) continues to forbid
  nonzero polynomial solutions.
* **Formal power series.** Airy's equation *does* admit formal power-series
  solutions in $\mathbb{R}[[x]]$, organized by the recurrence on coefficients
  induced by (1). Contrasting the polynomial nonexistence proved here with the
  power-series existence theory would give a complete picture of where, in the
  hierarchy of formal function classes, the solutions of Airy's equation first
  appear.

## 9. Conclusion

Airy's equation $y'' = x\,y$, for all its analytic depth, hides a purely
combinatorial secret: it cannot be solved by a polynomial, and neither can its
Riccati companion $u' + u^2 = x$. The proofs are short, elementary, and sharp —
a comparison of two integers, the degrees of the two sides — and they extend
without effort to a broad family of related equations and to any integral domain
of coefficients. They illustrate, in microcosm, how an algebraic reading of a
differential equation can settle a question about its solutions with finality
and economy.

## A curve that bends the rules

In 1838 the British astronomer George Biddell Airy was trying to understand
a stubborn optical puzzle: what exactly happens to light near a *caustic*, the
bright fold you see at the edge of a rainbow or shimmering on the bottom of a
coffee cup? The wave theory of light told him that the brightness should be
governed by a single, deceptively simple differential equation:

$$ y'' = x\,y. $$

In words: the curvature of the function $y$ at each point $x$ is equal to the
function's own value, multiplied by how far you are from the origin. To the
left of zero the equation behaves like the equation of a spring, producing
gentle oscillations; to the right of zero it behaves like a runaway
exponential. Right at the origin the two regimes meet, and the resulting
function — the **Airy function** — sits at the heart of optics, quantum
mechanics, and the theory of random matrices.

Airy's equation looks like it ought to be tame. After all, its right-hand side
is just "$x$ times $y$" — about as simple as a variable coefficient can be. So
here is a natural question, the kind a curious student might ask on first
meeting the equation:

> Is there a *polynomial* that solves Airy's equation?

A polynomial — something like $p(x) = 3x^4 - x + 7$ — is the friendliest kind
of function there is. It is built from a finite number of powers of $x$, it is
infinitely smooth, and we can differentiate it forever without leaving the
world of polynomials. Many famous differential equations have beautiful
polynomial solutions: Legendre's equation gives the Legendre polynomials,
Hermite's equation gives the Hermite polynomials, and so on. Could Airy's
equation hide a polynomial too?

The answer, it turns out, is a clean and total **no** — and the reason why is
a small gem of mathematical reasoning that requires nothing more than counting.

## Counting the degree

Every nonzero polynomial has a **degree**: the highest power of $x$ that
appears in it. The polynomial $3x^4 - x + 7$ has degree $4$; the constant $5$
has degree $0$. The degree is a kind of fingerprint, and it interacts with the
basic operations of algebra in completely predictable ways.

Two rules are all we need.

**Rule 1 — Multiplying by $x$ raises the degree by one.** If $p$ has degree
$n$, then $x \cdot p$ has degree $n+1$. Multiplying by $x$ shifts every term up
one power, so the top term $x^n$ becomes $x^{n+1}$. Nothing can cancel it.

**Rule 2 — Differentiating lowers the degree by (at least) one.** The
derivative of $x^n$ is $n\,x^{n-1}$, so taking a derivative knocks the degree
down by one. Differentiate *twice* and you lose at least two degrees: the
second derivative $p''$ has degree at most $n - 2$.

Now put the two sides of Airy's equation head to head. Suppose, for the sake of
argument, that some nonzero polynomial $p$ of degree $n$ satisfied $p'' = x\,p$.

* The **right-hand side**, $x \cdot p$, has degree $n + 1$ by Rule 1.
* The **left-hand side**, $p''$, has degree at most $n - 2$ by Rule 2.

But if two polynomials are equal, they must have the *same* degree. We would
need
$$ n + 1 \le n - 2, $$
which simplifies to $1 \le -2$. That is absurd. The right-hand side is always
*more* wiggly — higher degree — than the left-hand side can ever be. There is
no room for the two to meet.

The only escape hatch is the polynomial we quietly excluded at the start: the
**zero polynomial**, $p = 0$, which has no degree to compare and trivially
satisfies $0 = x \cdot 0$. And that is the whole story.

> **Theorem (No polynomial solutions of Airy's equation).** The only
> polynomial $p$ satisfying $p'' = x\,p$ is the zero polynomial $p = 0$.

What is striking is how little machinery the proof needs. No calculus of
limits, no infinite series, no clever substitution — just the observation that
multiplying by $x$ pushes a polynomial *up* the degree ladder while
differentiating pulls it *down*, and the two can never be reconciled.

## A second disguise: the Riccati form

Differential equations love disguises. A standard trick for studying a
second-order linear equation like Airy's is to look not at $y$ itself but at
the **logarithmic derivative** $u = y'/y$ — the relative rate at which $y$ is
growing. This substitution turns the linear equation into a *nonlinear* one
called a **Riccati equation**. For Airy's equation, the logarithmic-derivative
substitution produces

$$ u' + u^2 = x. $$

This is the same equation wearing a different costume. It is natural to ask the
same question of it: does the Riccati form admit a polynomial solution $u$? And
again the answer is a flat **no** — but now the degree-counting argument has a
small twist, because of that squared term $u^2$.

Suppose $u$ is a polynomial of degree $d$. We compare the degrees of the three
pieces.

* The term $u^2$ has degree $2d$, because squaring a polynomial doubles its
  degree.
* The term $u'$ has degree at most $d - 1$, one less than $u$.
* The right-hand side $x$ has degree exactly $1$.

Now split into two cases.

**Case 1: $u$ is a constant ($d = 0$).** Then $u'$ is zero and $u^2$ is a
constant, so the entire left-hand side $u' + u^2$ is a constant — degree $0$.
But the right-hand side $x$ has degree $1$. A constant can never equal $x$.
Contradiction.

**Case 2: $u$ has degree $d \ge 1$.** Now the squared term dominates
everything. Its degree $2d$ is at least $2$, and it strictly exceeds the degree
of $u'$ (which is at most $d-1 < 2d$). When you add a high-degree polynomial to
a strictly lower-degree one, the high degree survives — nothing cancels the top
term. So $u' + u^2$ has degree exactly $2d \ge 2$. But the right-hand side $x$
has degree $1$. Again the degrees cannot match.

Either way we reach a contradiction, and so:

> **Theorem (No polynomial solutions of the Riccati form).** There is no
> polynomial $u$ satisfying $u' + u^2 = x$.

Here there is not even a zero-polynomial escape hatch: the Riccati equation has
*no* polynomial solution whatsoever, not even the trivial one, because $0' +
0^2 = 0 \ne x$.

## Why this matters

It would be easy to dismiss these results as negative trivia — "this equation
doesn't have *that* kind of solution, so what?" But absence theorems are some
of the most useful tools in mathematics, precisely because they tell you where
*not* to look.

The Airy function genuinely exists; it is smooth, well-behaved, and central to
physics. What our two theorems prove is that this function lives *outside* the
cozy world of polynomials. No amount of algebraic cleverness — no finite
combination of powers of $x$ — will ever capture it. To write the Airy function
down you are forced into richer territory: infinite power series, integrals,
or special transcendental functions. The simplicity of the equation is a kind
of trap; its solutions are irreducibly more complicated than the equation that
defines them.

This is a recurring theme across mathematics and physics. The pendulum's exact
period cannot be written with elementary functions. The orbit of three
gravitating bodies has no closed-form solution. Time and again, a short,
innocent-looking equation turns out to demand answers that no finite formula
can express. The degree-counting proof for Airy's equation is a miniature,
fully rigorous instance of this phenomenon — and one you can verify with pencil
and paper in a single sitting.

Step back and notice the architecture of both proofs, because the same skeleton
appears throughout the study of differential equations with polynomial
coefficients.

1. **Assume a polynomial solution exists**, and give its degree a name.
2. **Track how each operation moves the degree.** Multiplication by $x$ adds

3. **Compare the two sides of the equation.** If they are forced to have

immediately. Replace $x$ by any polynomial coefficient $q(x)$ of degree at
least one, and the equation $p'' = q\,p$ still has no nonzero polynomial
solution, by exactly the same imbalance: the right-hand side outpaces the left.
Push to higher derivatives, $p^{(k)} = x\,p$, and the gap only widens. The
single idea — *that some operations build polynomials up faster than others can
tear them down* — rules out an entire family of would-be solutions in one
stroke.

Airy set out to explain a band of light at the edge of a rainbow. Two hundred
years later, the equation he wrote down still rewards a fresh look — and one of
its secrets, that it can never be solved by a polynomial, turns out to rest on
nothing deeper than knowing how to count.
